title: Understanding Public Budgets
tagline: Where public money comes from and how it is spent.
description: Public budgets decide which services get funded. Learn in plain language where the money comes from, how a budget is decided, and how to ask informed questions about spending in your area.
outcomes: Understand where public money comes from
Follow the basic steps of how a budget is decided
Know where citizens can give input
Ask clear, informed questions about spending

lessons.title: Where public money comes from
lessons.body:
Public services are paid for with money the public provides.

## The main sources
Most public money comes from taxes (like income tax and VAT) and from fees and levies (like trading fees and licences). Some comes from grants and loans. This pooled money pays for clinics, schools, roads and more.

## Why it matters
Because it is public money, the public has a fair interest in how it is spent and a right to ask informed questions.
key_points: Public money comes mainly from taxes and fees
Some comes from grants and loans
Public money means the public can ask how it is spent
lessons.try_it: List two services in your area that are paid for with public money.

lessons.title: How a budget is decided
lessons.body:
A budget is a plan for spending over a year. It follows a cycle.

## The basic cycle
Offices propose what they need. Plans are reviewed and approved by the council or national level. Money is released and spent. At the end, spending is reported and checked.

## Where citizens fit
Public consultations and ward meetings are points where residents can give input before a budget is finalised. Showing up at the right time is how your needs get heard.
key_points: A budget is a yearly spending plan
It follows propose, approve, spend, report
Consultations are where citizens give input
Timing matters — give input before it is finalised
lessons.try_it: Find out when budget or ward planning meetings happen in your area.

lessons.title: Asking good questions about spending
lessons.body:
You do not need to be an expert to ask useful questions.

## Good questions are specific
Ask about one project: How much was budgeted? How much has been spent? What was delivered? When will it be finished? Specific questions are easier to answer and harder to dodge.

## Stay factual and fair
Ask for figures and dates, not blame. Keep a note of answers. If figures are public, you have a right to see them.
key_points: Focus each question on one project
Ask budgeted vs spent, and what was delivered
Ask for figures and dates, not blame
Keep a note of the answers you get
lessons.try_it: Write two specific questions about a project you can see in your area.

quiz.question: Where does most public money come from?
quiz.explanation: Most public money comes from taxes, plus fees and levies, with some grants and loans.

quiz.question: A good question about a project is:
options: How much was budgeted and spent, and what was delivered?
quiz.explanation: Specific questions about budgeted vs spent and what was delivered are clear and fair.
